headline: Court backs Missouri's new map. Ballots are already out.
summary: A federal appeals panel ruled Monday that Missouri must use its new Republican-drawn House map in November, the one Trump backed and the Supreme Court has twice blocked. Nothing changes yet: the order waits a week for an appeal, and opponents say they will go straight to the Supreme Court. Absentee ballots with the old districts are already out.

cover_question.q: Isn't it too late to change the map?

cover_answer: The clerks say so. The Supreme Court gets the last word.
table_question: Can you change the rules after the game has started?

5-7.chip: Bring it up if it fits the day
5-7.script: Missouri drew new lines on its voting map. The lines sort people into groups, and each group picks one person for Congress, like sorting a class into teams. On Monday some judges said use the new lines. The top court in the country has said wait, and some people already voted, so the grown-ups are sorting it out.
5-7.why: Teams in a class is a picture. A district is not. At this age a child needs the one thing they can see, and the fight over lines is it.
5-7.why_long: A five-year-old reasons from what is in front of them, so the script turns a district into a team drawn from the class, the one part of this they can picture. Which judge said what stays out. Expect "who's the boss of the judges?" The top court in the country, and it has said wait.

8-12.chip: Bring it up if it fits the day
8-12.script: Missouri drew a new voting map, the one Trump wanted. The Supreme Court blocked it twice, so absentee ballots went out with the old map. On Monday an appeals court said use the new map anyway, because the August primary did. Two referees disagree, and the head referee gets the last call.
8-12.why: A chain with a rule at the end, and two referees who disagree.
8-12.why_long: This age is working out cause and effect and whether adults apply rules consistently, and the story is a chain they can follow: a new map, a block, ballots out, a court saying use it anyway. Two referees is the mechanism; the head referee is the Supreme Court. Expect "so who's right?" The head referee decides. That is the rule.

13-17.script: Can a state change its map after voting has started? An appeals court says Missouri must use its Trump-backed map because the August primary did, though the Supreme Court has blocked it twice. Second: two of the three judges are Trump appointees. Does that change your reading?
13-17.why: Two true things: the primary used the new map, the ballots use the old.
13-17.why_long: A teenager can hold two true things at once, and the ruling asks for it: the August primary used the new map, and the November ballots already out use the old one. Then the harder pair: a ruling can be reasoned and the judge can still have been Trump's lawyer. Expect "is it rigged?" Say what you know. The Hill calls the map 7-1.

5-7.q: Do the lines change who wins?
5-7.a: They can. That's why both sides care so much about where the lines go.

8-12.q: Why does it matter where the lines are?
8-12.a: They decide who votes together. Move them and a different side wins. The Hill calls it a 7-1 map.
The Supreme Court. It has blocked this map twice already.

13-17.q: Isn't it too late to change the map?
13-17.a: The appeals court says yes. The clerks say practically impossible.

13-17.q: Does it matter who picked the judges?
13-17.a: Two of three are Trump appointees. Does that change the reading?
